cards.title: The State of Context Engineering

depth.text: someone explains why **AI agents** get stuck with too much context, and why **forgetting** can help

The talk names **four failure modes** for long context—poisoning, distraction, confusion and clash. It calls agents’ tendency to keep pursuing a subtask after they should stop **context inertia**; Anthropic’s fix is to clear the conversation while preserving the work.

cards.camps: Two camps: some say long contexts make models seem dumber and resets help; others say newer models need the extra context and don’t degrade much until much later.

comments.text: It's nice that this article goes beyond the "context too long" scapegoat diagnostic. There is more to it than just reducing content in context. LLMs attention mechanism works by finding graphs of related words and concepts and it works best when the relevant relationships are close together in the text. Length matters but how well the information is organized matters as well. It's useful to be…

I like the idea of VictorTaelin's UniiChat [1] which summarizes every message into a single line and on top of that a binary tree of lines combined from lower levels. The context is then a view of that tree with more detail in recent messages and less detail in historical messages, plus a `zoom` tool that enables the agent to navigate the tree and read messages. An implementation of this idea…

Very informative article but why this term coining? The phenomena and strategies aren't specific to LLMs but are well known from other areas of computer science (and psychology). For example, I would have called "offloading" just "swapping", and "confusion" just "pollution".

> As we focus more on memory, we also need to think about strategic forgetting. Over time, overly precise memories become conflicted and messy, and nobody has yet figured out how to handle this. > I think that’s the context problem of tomorrow. cards.title: Birdwatching rewires the brain and slows cognitive decline

depth.text: **birdwatching** may help keep the **brain organised** and slow **age-related decline**

Erik Wing compared **MRI scans** from expert birders and novices while they identified birds. Some regions in experts’ brains were **more organised** than in novices of the same age. The study **can’t tell** whether birdwatching caused those differences or the differences came first.

cards.camps: Two camps: some suspect birdwatching’s learning and curiosity matter; others think nature, walking, socialising or any stimulating hobby could explain the benefits.
entities: Baycrest Academy for Research and Education

cards.title: Moderna and Merck say their mRNA cancer vaccine cut death, recurrence by 42%

depth.text: Moderna and Merck say a **personalized cancer vaccine** lowered melanoma patients’ **risk of death or recurrence**

In a Phase 3 trial of 1,137 patients whose melanoma had been surgically removed, adding intismeran to Keytruda lowered the risk of recurrence or death by **42 percent** after two years. **82 percent** of that group were alive without recurrence, versus **70 percent** with Keytruda and a placebo.
data: Risk reduction in recurrence or death
Risk reduction in distant metastasis or death

comments.text: Moderna's business model was always to be an on-demand vaccine platform, meaning a cost-effective service for ordering a few doses of a fully custom personalized vaccine. Their infrastructure looks more like a just-in-time 3D printer service than like a traditional vaccine development lab. It was a happy accident that the platform was available when we needed to come up with a COVID vaccine…

The Trump administration and RFK Jr. are actively working to prevent mRNA vaccines from reaching the market. People like Marc Andreessen, Larry Ellison and Elon Musk are actively supporting the administration, including hundreds of millions in donations to MAGA political campaigns in recent months. Should we hold these people accountable for the damage they're indirectly doing to public health?…

Amazingly, when this (IMHO quite good) data leaked, Moderna stock took a huge drop: https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article/moderna-sto ...
(Seems like people were expecting absolutely incredible, "cure for cancer" results and had already bid up the price a lot in advance.)
Related, if you are curious: this is what BioNTech is currently working on. https://www.biontech.com/int/en/home/pipeline-and-products/p...

So the absolute risk of recurrence/death on Keytruda alone was 30%, reduced to 18% with Keytruda plus intismeran. That will definitely make a noticeable difference in this disease if the real world results hold.

cards.title: Why I Am a Programmer

depth.text: someone found **demos** through **pirated games** and wanted to make those **dazzling effects** themselves

He edited saved-game files for **unlimited lives** and skipped stages, then got a modem and explored BBSes. Downloaded games played **cracktros** before their title screens; later, Denthor's **tutorials** showed him how to code demo-like effects in Pascal.

comments.text: Conan the Barbarian and Below the Root on our Apple IIe. Tiny worlds behind the glowing Orange CRT. How do I make something like this? My mum (lol) helped me figure out how to get keyboard input in BASIC. I made a little game where an O character chases your X character around the screen. Core game loop. Browsing pirate CGA games at the warung in Pondok Indah, well outside the jurisdiction of US…

Getting to build things without skinned knuckles or solder smoke in your face... now that is a rush! And if you are not happy with it, you get to tear it down and build it back up better. It costs nothing but your time and imagination. Importantly, you get to build, to solve problems, to engineer, to visualize, to create and be creative. (Ok, maybe musicians have even more fun, but alas I wasn't…

For me, it was the creative, puzzle-solving, game-like nature of it. Then I got my first job, and I had 100% autonomy, so a friend of mine and I got to solve real problems for real people in the real world. It was a rush. Making people’s lives better through software is still the biggest motivation for me.
(2015) Even links to the HN discussion at the time (89 points, 59 comments) https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=8837545

cards.title: Bbtree: Fastest Ordered Map

depth.text: one commenter tried a **new ordered map** and found it **slower in several workloads**

Swapping out std::BTreeMap made **union/difference +11% to +21% slower** and the **intersection stage +16% to +34% slower** in one 3D mesh test. A separate dictionary-words test found map<String, usize> used **40% more RAM** than std::collections::BtreeMap; commenters also questioned whether “fastest” holds across workloads.

comments.text:
Your mileage may vary. I tested this on a 3D boolean mesh kernel I am working on (this is swapping out std::BTreeMap, no other code changes): ┌────────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────┐

glossary.open weight models: AI models whose internal settings are shared so others can run or change them.
glossary.on-prem: Software that runs on a company's own computers rather than being accessed as an online service.
glossary.frontier models: The most capable AI models a company is developing.
glossary.token: A chunk of text an AI reads or writes, often a whole word or part of one.
glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: the chip part that draws images and video.
glossary.rack: A frame that holds servers and other computer equipment together.
glossary.vector format: A way to make images from shapes so they stay sharp when resized.
glossary.CJK fonts: Chinese, Japanese, and Korean fonts: typefaces that include characters used to write those languages.
glossary.CSS: Cascading Style Sheets: rules that control how a web page looks.
glossary.SVG: Scalable Vector Graphics: a picture format that stays sharp when resized.
glossary.dot-matrix printer: A printer that makes letters and pictures by striking an ink ribbon with tiny pins.
glossary.VM: Virtual machine: a computer that runs inside another computer.
glossary.geodata: Information about real places, like their height, water, roads and forests.
glossary.Cubic Chunks: A Minecraft add-on that lets the game build places beyond its usual height limit.
glossary.mod: A way to keep only the remainder after dividing one number by another.
glossary.Early Access: A version people can play while its maker is still working on it.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.voxel: A small block used to build a 3D image, like a pixel with depth.
glossary.context window: The amount of text and information an AI can take into account at one time.
glossary.context inertia: When an AI gets fixated on an idea or task and keeps pursuing it after it should stop.
glossary.context poisoning: Bad or irrelevant information gets into an AI’s working conversation and steers its answer.
glossary.harness: The surrounding code that gives an AI agent tools and a place to work, and checks what it does.
glossary.compaction: Shortening an AI’s conversation history, often by turning it into a summary.
glossary.weights: Stored values a trained network uses when it works out what to produce.
glossary.RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation: a way for an AI to look up material and use it when answering.
glossary.deterministic: Something that gives the same result when it gets the same input.
glossary.probabilistic: Able to give different results because chance is involved.
glossary.dependency length: How far apart words that belong together are in a sentence; shorter gaps can make the meaning easier to follow.
glossary.1u: A keyboard-size unit; the project says its 1u boards are 19.05 mm square.
glossary.PCB: Printed Circuit Board: a flat board that holds electronic parts and connects them with metal paths.
glossary.pogo pins: Spring-loaded metal contacts that touch another part to make an electrical connection.
glossary.I2C: Inter-Integrated Circuit: a way for electronic parts to exchange messages using shared wires.
glossary.firmware: The built-in software that tells a device's hardware how to work.
glossary.microcontroller: A tiny computer inside a device that tells the device what to do.
glossary.POC: Proof of Concept: a small test or demo that checks whether an idea can work.
glossary.MRI: Magnetic resonance imaging: a scan that uses magnets to make pictures of the inside of the body.
glossary.neuroplasticity: The brain’s ability to change how it works and is organised over time.
glossary.cognitive decline: A worsening ability to remember, think clearly or follow a conversation.
glossary.confounding factor: Something else that may explain a result, making it hard to know what caused it.
glossary.MCP: Model Context Protocol: a standard way for AI apps to connect to outside tools.
glossary.REST: A common way for one app to send requests to another app over a network.
glossary.OCR: Optical character recognition: software that reads words from a picture or scanned page.
glossary.PII: Personally Identifiable Information: details that could identify someone, such as an email or phone number.
glossary.WASM: WebAssembly: a way for an app to run plug-ins written in other programming languages.
glossary.Rust: A programming language; commenters say 37signals used it for the Hey backend.
glossary.S-1: A filing that gives investors details about a company's finances and share offering before an IPO.
glossary.open-weight models: AI models whose learned settings are made available for others to use or change.
glossary.compute: The processing power computers use to run AI or other software.
glossary.net loss: When a company spends more than it earns over a reporting period.
glossary.operating profit: Money left from a company's main business after its operating costs are paid.
glossary.stock-based compensation: Paying workers partly with shares in the company instead of cash.
glossary.IPO: Initial Public Offering: when a company first offers its shares for the public to buy.
glossary.Lighthouse: A tool that checks a web page’s speed and other quality measures.
glossary.framework: A collection of ready-made parts and rules that helps people build software.
glossary.static site: A website made of ready-to-serve pages, rather than pages generated anew for each visit.
glossary.CDN: Content Delivery Network: A network of servers that helps websites handle requests closer to their users.
glossary.ISR: Incremental Static Regeneration: a way to refresh already-built pages after a site is published.
glossary.hydration: JavaScript adding the behavior that makes a page’s controls work after its HTML loads.
glossary.server components: Parts of a website that run on the site’s server instead of in a visitor’s browser.
glossary.SEO: Search engine optimization: making changes to a webpage so it is more likely to appear in search results.
glossary.NeXTSTEP: The main software that ran NeXT computers and gave people the screens and tools they used.
glossary.sequence: A section of a film made up of several shots.
glossary.shot: A stretch of a film made with one camera setup.
glossary.frame: One still picture in a film; shown quickly with others, it looks like movement.
glossary.stereo 3D: A way to show different images to the left and right eyes so the picture looks deep.
glossary.pipeline: A series of steps where each step works on data and passes it to the next.
glossary.rig: A setup that lets animators move a digital character.
glossary.FTP: File Transfer Protocol: a way to move files between your computer and a server.
glossary.webmail: Email you use through a website instead of an app on your device.
glossary.DNS: Domain Name System: the internet's address book, which helps a computer find a website from its name.
glossary.ISP: Internet Service Provider: a company that connects people to the internet.
glossary.VPN: Virtual private network: a service that sends your internet traffic through another computer, often to protect it or make it appear to come from somewhere else.
glossary.DoH: DNS over HTTPS: a way to send website-name lookups through a protected web connection.
glossary.DoT: DNS over TLS: a way to protect website-name lookups as they travel over the internet.
glossary.run-off election: An extra election round where voters choose between candidates after an earlier round leaves no winner.
glossary.open-weight model: A model whose trained settings are shared so other people can use them.
glossary.inference provider: A service that runs an AI model and sends its replies to an app.
glossary.cache read: Reusing saved text from earlier in a conversation instead of processing it all over again.
glossary.grading on completion: A teacher checks whether you turned the work in, rather than whether every answer is right.
glossary.AI agents: Computer programs that can carry out tasks, rather than only answer a question.
glossary.git worktree: A separate working copy of a project, so you can work on another task without mixing up files.
glossary.living specs: Project notes that describe what the software is meant to do and are updated as it changes.
glossary.CLI: Command-Line Interface: a way to control a computer by typing commands instead of clicking buttons.
glossary.pi: The coding agent ThinkRail runs to work on code.
glossary.mRNA: Messenger RNA: instructions that cells can use to make proteins.
glossary.Phase 3 trial: A later-stage test in people that compares a treatment with the usual care or another option.
glossary.intismeran: The name of the personalized mRNA vaccine used with Keytruda in this trial.
glossary.Keytruda: Merck’s cancer treatment used as the standard treatment in this trial.
glossary.placebo: A treatment with no active study drug, used so researchers can compare it with the drug being tested.
glossary.RFS: Recurrence-free survival: how long a patient goes without the cancer returning.
glossary.DMFS: Distant metastasis-free survival: how long a patient goes without the cancer returning in a different part of the body.
glossary.monoclonal antibody: A lab-made medicine designed to latch onto one particular target in the body.
glossary.BBS: Bulletin Board System: an online place people used to post messages and share files.
glossary.cracktro: A short intro that plays before a game, made by people who cracked its copy protection.
glossary.demo: A short computer-made display of visual effects, made to show what its creators can do.
glossary.demoscene: A community where people make computer demos to show off skill and creativity.
glossary.Hex View: A way to see a file's contents as numbers and change them.
glossary.Pascal: A programming language used in Denthor's tutorials.
glossary.ordered map: A collection that stores items in a chosen order and lets a program find one by its label.
glossary.B-tree: A way of keeping sorted items in a tree-shaped layout so a program can find them quickly.
glossary.trie: A way to organize words by their shared beginnings so software can find matching words quickly.
glossary.DRAM: Dynamic Random-Access Memory: the working memory a computer uses while running things.
